name: JavaScript
tagline: The scripting language that powers interactive web experiences.
timeTravelLog: Coded in 10 days in 1995 by Brendan Eich. It turned static pages into interactive, responsive applications.
overview: JavaScript is a powerful, lightweight, interpreted scripting language with first-class functions. It powers interactivity, fetches real-time data, and controls every dynamic behavior of modern web applications.

syllabus.title: Module 1: Variables & Data Types
syllabus.desc: How scripts store intelligence in named memory addresses.
syllabus.content: Variables store data in memory. Use const for values that never change and let for values that will. Never use var in modern JS — it causes scope leaks. JavaScript has 7 primitive datatypes: String, Number, Boolean, Null, Undefined, BigInt, and Symbol. Objects and Arrays are reference types that can hold collections.
syllabus.codeExample:
const userName = 'Jesmon';    // String
let usageLevel = 98;             // Number
let isAutoSyncOn = false;     // Boolean
const coordinates = null;       // Null

const regions = ['Alpha', 'Beta', 'Gamma'];  // Array
const app = { code: 'JES-01', speed: 12 };     // Object
syllabus.interactiveTip: Use camelCase for all variable names (usageLevel, not usage_level). Names must start with a letter, underscore, or dollar sign — never a number.

syllabus.title: Module 2: Functions (Reusable Logic Blocks)
syllabus.desc: Writing reusable functions that compute results from inputs.
syllabus.content: Functions are named or anonymous blocks of code that can be called repeatedly. They accept parameters (inputs) and return results via the return keyword. Modern JS uses arrow function syntax which is shorter and lexically scopes the 'this' keyword — essential for working inside class methods and callbacks.
syllabus.interactiveTip: Arrow functions with a single expression body don't need curly braces or a return statement — the expression value is returned implicitly!

syllabus.title: Module 3: Conditionals & Switch Cases
syllabus.desc: Executing branching decisions based on real-time system evaluations.
syllabus.content: Conditionals allow scripts to make decisions. if/else evaluates boolean expressions. Ternary operators (condition ? trueValue : falseValue) are compact single-line alternatives. Switch statements handle multiple fixed values cleanly without deeply nested if-else chains.
syllabus.interactiveTip: Always include a default case in switch statements to handle unexpected values gracefully — just like a fallback behavior in project systems!

syllabus.title: Module 4: Arrays & Objects
syllabus.desc: Organizing, reading, and mutating collections of structured data.
syllabus.content: Arrays store ordered lists and are accessed by index (starting at 0). Objects store key-value pairs and are accessed via dot notation (obj.key) or bracket notation (obj['key']). Both are reference types — modifying a copy also modifies the original unless you spread-clone them.
syllabus.interactiveTip: Use the spread operator (...) to clone arrays and objects without mutation: const newTeam = [...team, 'Orion'] creates a safe copy with an added item!

syllabus.title: Module 5: Loops (For, While & Higher-Order Functions)
syllabus.desc: Iterating through data streams and transforming collections.
syllabus.content: Loops execute blocks repeatedly. for loops iterate a fixed number of times. for...of iterates array values. for...in iterates object keys. But the most powerful are higher-order array methods: .map() transforms every item, .filter() returns only matching items, .find() returns the first match, .reduce() computes a single result from all items.
syllabus.interactiveTip: Prefer .map(), .filter() and .reduce() over manual for loops when transforming arrays — they are cleaner, chainable, and side-effect free!

syllabus.title: Module 6: DOM Manipulation (Document Object Model)
syllabus.desc: Reading, modifying, and controlling the live HTML structure from scripts.
syllabus.content: The DOM (Document Object Model) is a live tree representation of your HTML page that JavaScript can read and modify. document.querySelector() selects the first matching element. classList.add/remove/toggle manages CSS classes. innerHTML and textContent update element content. createElement() and appendChild() build new nodes dynamically.
syllabus.interactiveTip: Use querySelectorAll() to select multiple elements and iterate them with .forEach(). It returns a NodeList, not an Array — but forEach still works on it!

syllabus.title: Module 7: Async JavaScript (Events, Fetch API & Promises)
syllabus.desc: Listening to user interactions and loading live data without page reloads.
syllabus.content: addEventListener attaches event handlers for clicks, keypresses, form submissions, and more. The Fetch API loads remote data asynchronously, returning a Promise. Promises represent eventual results — .then() chains success, .catch() handles errors. async/await syntax makes Promises read like synchronous code for cleaner, more readable asynchronous engineering.
syllabus.interactiveTip: Always wrap fetch calls in try/catch when using async/await — network failures and bad status codes will cause unhandled rejections that crash your interface!

quiz.question: Which keyword declares a variable that CANNOT be reassigned?
quiz.explanation: 'const' creates a block-scoped, read-only binding. The variable reference cannot be reassigned, though object/array contents can still be mutated.

quiz.question: What does the .filter() array method return?
options: A transformed copy of every element
A new array containing only elements that pass the test
A single computed value from all elements
quiz.explanation: .filter() returns a new array containing only elements for which the callback function returned true. It never mutates the original array.

quiz.question: Which method selects the first matching HTML element from the DOM?
quiz.explanation: document.querySelector() uses CSS selector syntax to find and return the first matching DOM element. It's the modern replacement for getElementById and getElementsByClassName.

quest.title: Project: Build a Usage Tracker
quest.challenge: Build an interactive dashboard that tracks usage levels, warns on low levels, and logs each update.
instructions: 1. Declare a let variable 'usage' starting at 100.
2. Create a button that reduces usage by 15 on each click.
3. Display the current usage level in a div after each click.
4. If usage drops below 20, change the display color to red and show a CRITICAL warning.
5. Add a 'Reset' button that restores usage back to 100.
